section.p: Mara found the brass lantern beneath a loose board in the old ferry house. It was small enough to hold in one hand, but its glass was clear and bright. A note tied to the handle said, Take this to the north pier before the fog comes in. No name followed, and no one in the village admitted leaving it. Mara lit the wick and watched a calm gold circle spread across the dusty floor. Outside, gulls turned above the harbor, and the tide was already beginning to rise. She remembered her grandmother saying that every harbor light was a promise: someone was watching, and someone would find the shore. Mara tucked the note into her coat and closed the ferry house door behind her.

She carried the lantern along the seawall as evening settled over the roofs. At the north pier, a little wooden boat bumped softly against its rope. An old man stood beside it, holding a map that the damp air had curled at the edges. He looked relieved when he saw the light. My sister is waiting across the inlet, he explained. The fog hides the channel markers, and I cannot leave without a guide. Mara set the lantern in the bow, where its reflection made a narrow road across the dark water. The man offered her the map, but she knew these waters from summers spent rowing with her father. She pointed toward the quiet gap between two black rocks and told him to keep the lantern in sight. Then she pushed the boat gently away from the pier.

The boat moved slowly, following the lantern's trembling path. From the shore, Mara could just make out a second light answering from the far bank. The old man raised one hand, and the boat turned toward it. When it reached the landing, a woman stepped forward and laughed with joy. They had been apart for many years, but they recognized each other at once. Mara waited until both were safely ashore, then carried the empty lantern home. At dawn she found a fresh note beneath her door: The light is yours whenever someone needs help finding the way. This time, it bore no signature either. Mara cleaned the lantern and placed it by the window, ready for another night.
